name: Vaseline on lashes/brows

lead: People dab petroleum jelly on lashes and brows as an inexpensive conditioner so the hairs look glossier and fuller. The sheen is visible right away.

Petroleum jelly forms an occlusive coating that reduces moisture loss and adds shine; it does not act on hair follicles. Lash length is largely set by genetics, and the only FDA-approved drug for lash growth is bimatoprost. No human studies in the sources tested it for growth, so claims that it grows more hair come from user reports.

paras: People apply a small amount with a clean spoolie or fingertip along lashes and brows, often at night, as part of a conditioning routine.
It can cause irritation if it gets in the eye, and some petroleum jelly products can contain trace hydrocarbons that regulators have commented on.

angle.text: People dab petroleum jelly on lashes and brows as a cheap conditioner so the hairs look glossier and fuller. The sheen shows right away. Claims that it grows more hair come from user reports; no studies tested it.

lead: Applying petroleum jelly (Vaseline is the best-known brand) to eyelashes and eyebrows is a cheap grooming practice used to make lashes and brows look glossier, darker and fuller. Users describe it as a conditioner that smooths and coats hairs, and some say it helps lashes appear longer over time.

Petroleum jelly is a semi-solid hydrocarbon mixture used in skin products as an occlusive that reduces moisture loss and friction. Eyelash length is largely set by genetics: upper lashes typically measure 7 to 8 mm and follicle numbers are fixed before birth [1].

No published human study has tested petroleum jelly for lash or brow length or density. The only FDA-approved drug for lash growth is bimatoprost (Latisse, introduced 2009), a prescription product [1].
infobox: Mostly genetic; upper lashes typically 7-8 mm [1]

paras: Petroleum jelly is mainly a skin protectant and occlusive, used in lotions and cosmetics to reduce moisture loss and friction. Proponents of using it on lashes and brows describe it as a cheap conditioner that makes hairs look shinier and may protect them.

Wikipedia reports that lashes do not continually grow like scalp hair, that length is mostly genetic and that follicle numbers are set in embryonic development [1]. Bimatoprost is described as the first FDA-approved lash growth drug; its maker reports noticeable growth within 16 weeks and up to a 25 percent increase in length [1]. Serum and conditioner brands use seed extracts, minerals or peptides, and curlers and extensions change apparent length without physically lengthening lashes [1]. The petroleum jelly article describes a moisture-retaining skin protectant and does not mention lash or brow use.

The petroleum jelly article notes that it can contain mineral oil aromatic hydrocarbons, and that European Food Safety Authority and consumer-testing reports raised concerns about contamination in some products. Products used near the eye can cause irritation; no data specific to lashes were found.

timeline.event: Latisse (bimatoprost) becomes the first FDA-approved drug for eyelash growth [1].
